% --------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Vertical balance and the frame ending (G2, G6, G9)
%   \FrameTop          first token of every frame body: stretch above the content
%   body / figure -> \Interp -> \SourceNote -> \Backups (or \BackTo, \BackToTwo)
% The content block is centred between the title bar and the note/button rows:
% \FrameTop and the glue before the note block (or, without a note, before the
% buttons) share the free space. The note block sits on the row just above the
% buttons, which sit on the last row above the footer (PI directive 8).
% Every \SourceNote is followed by \Backups, \BackTo or \BackToTwo in the same
% frame (lint_deck.py checks this).
% --------------------------------------------------------------------------
% \FrameTop takes back 0.15 cm of beamer's fixed 0.2 cm [t] top skip, so the block
% sits optically centred (measured: equal stretch alone left the top gap 0.27 cm
% larger than the bottom gap on every slide).
\newif\ifdeckSrc
\newcommand{\FrameTop}{\global\deckSrcfalse\vskip -0.15cm plus 1filll\relax}
% Final fixer (7 Oct 2026): at 8.0 pt most notes run to 2 lines. To make room, the button row is set on the
% button font's own leading (\DeckBtnRow: the buttons stay on the same last row; only the dead glue above
% them goes), \Interp sits 0.06 cm under the figure (was 0.15), and the note keeps a fixed 0.06 cm from the
% text above it, so it never touches the \Interp lines on a full slide. The note is \raggedright (not
% ragged2e's \RaggedRight, whose 2em stretch let an unbreakable 'Benjamini--Hochberg' overrun the line).
\newcommand{\SourceNote}[1]{\par\vskip 0.06cm plus 1filll\relax
  {\color{Muted}\FsNote\raggedright #1\par}\vspace{0.12cm}\global\deckSrctrue}
\newcommand{\DeckNavGlue}{\par\ifdeckSrc\else\vskip 0pt plus 1filll\relax\fi\global\deckSrcfalse}
\newcommand{\Interp}[1]{\par\vspace{0.06cm}{\centering\color{Ink}\FsBody #1\par}}
\newcommand{\BL}[2]{\hyperlink{#1}{\beamergotobutton{#2}}\hspace{0.15cm}\ignorespaces}
\newcommand{\DeckBtnRow}{\usebeamerfont{button}\baselineskip=8.4pt\relax}
\newcommand{\Backups}[1]{\DeckNavGlue{\DeckBtnRow\noindent\hfill#1\unskip\par}}
% Return links. In the short build (main_short.tex) a backup may point back to
% a main slide that the short path omits; the link then goes to the backup
% index instead, so every link resolves in both builds. The footer carries
% the "Backup index" link on every backup.
\makeatletter
\providecommand{\ShortLabels}{}
\newcommand{\bt@target}{}
\newcommand{\bt@set}[1]{%
  \ifdefined\ShortPath
    \@expandtwoargs\in@{,#1,}{,\ShortLabels,}%
    \ifin@\def\bt@target{#1}\else\def\bt@target{B-index}\fi
  \else\def\bt@target{#1}\fi}
\newcommand{\BackTo}[2]{%
  \DeckNavGlue{\DeckBtnRow\noindent\hfill
  \bt@set{#1}\hyperlink{\bt@target}{\beamerreturnbutton{#2}}\par}}
\newcommand{\BackToTwo}[4]{%
  \DeckNavGlue{\DeckBtnRow\noindent\hfill
  \bt@set{#1}\hyperlink{\bt@target}{\beamerreturnbutton{#2}}%
  \hspace{0.15cm}\bt@set{#3}\hyperlink{\bt@target}{\beamerreturnbutton{#4}}\par}}
\makeatother

% Note numbers: [S1] 1,020 PMEs; [S2] 397 people involved in PME hiring or manpower decisions; [S5, S6] mirrored choices on a common menu
% Removed from the round-4 note, pending the PI: "the analysis and options are the SMU team's" - a governance fact, see B-governance
\note{[Short path] Colleagues from MOM, NTUC and SNEF: the question for Singapore is no longer whether flexible work exists, but which arrangements can retain PMEs while remaining workable for firms.
In this joint study with SNEF, 1,020 PMEs and 465 people involved in PME hiring or manpower decisions made mirrored choices on a common menu of arrangements. % [S1, S2, S5]
The results point to common ground, a role-dependent case, and arrangements that need testing before scaling.
Values in per cent of pay are a measuring rod, not a proposal to lower pay.
The findings are preliminary; we end with points for discussion.
[Timing: 130 words a minute plus 15 seconds a slide. Short path, 15 slides, target 17 to 18 minutes: Title, Motivation, Question, Framework, Design, PMEs, Why PMEs, Employers, Where, Meet, Compressed week, Barriers, Options, Conclusion, Thank you. % Note numbers: [P4s] 28 in 2008, 73 in mid-2024, establishments with 25 or more staff, private plus public sector;
% [P4, P4s] 66 in 2025 and 68 in 2023, both MOM's odd-year Supplementary Survey; [P6] fewer working-age residents per senior, no number spoken
\note{[Short path] Flexible work is now mainstream. In 2008, 28 per cent of establishments with 25 or more staff offered a scheduled flexible arrangement; by mid-2024, 73 per cent did. % [P4s]
The 2025 reading, 66 per cent, comes from MOM's odd-year survey, which gave 68 in 2023; we do not read the change as an effect of the Guidelines. % [P4, P4s]
With fewer working-age residents per senior, keeping people in work matters more. % [P6]
But a firm offering one arrangement may not offer the one a worker values, or one the role can sustain.
So the partners' question is no longer how many firms offer flexibility, but which arrangements, for which roles, on what terms; MOM's surveys are well placed to track that.
That points to three open problems.}

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-intl]{Remote work: Singapore and abroad}
  \FrameTop
  {\FsBody\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.05}
  \begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.1cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.7cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{1.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{1.4cm}@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Definition} & \textbf{Population} & \textbf{Country} & \textbf{Value} & \textbf{Year}\\
    \midrule
    \multirow{6}{3.1cm}{\raggedright Days worked from home last week (6+ hours)}
      & \multirow{6}{2.7cm}{\raggedright Full-time workers aged 20--64 with a college degree}
      & Average of 40 countries & 1.2 & 2024/25\\
      & & \textbf{Singapore} & \textbf{1.2} & 2024/25\\
      & & United Kingdom & 1.8 & 2024/25\\
      & & United States & 1.6 & 2024/25\\
      & & Japan & 0.7 & 2024/25\\
      & & South Korea & 0.5 & 2024/25\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabularx}\par}
  \SourceNote{Same survey and question in every country. Aksoy et al.\ 2025 (EconPol Policy Brief 73, Fig.\ 1).}
  \Backups{\BL{B-references}{Studies} \BL{M-intl-wtp}{Benchmarks}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] Flexible work is mainstream in Singapore's firms, but how much remote work do people actually do compared with elsewhere? % [P4s]
In the Global Survey of Working Arrangements (Aksoy et al. 2025; 16,422 college-educated full-time workers in 40 countries, November 2024 to February 2025), people work from home 1.2 days a week on average. Singapore is at that average, 1.2; the UK is at 1.8 and the US at 1.6, while Japan is at 0.7 and South Korea at 0.5. The same question and sample definition are used in every country. % [Aksoy et al. 2025, Fig. 1]
So remote work in Singapore is at the 40-country average, below the UK and US and above Japan and South Korea. The open question is therefore less how much remote work there is, and more which arrangements fit which workers and roles; the value of WFH, compared with studies elsewhere, comes after our results.
}

% Note numbers: none spoken. Context only: [P1] the Guidelines set a process; [P2] no administrative request counts;
% [P3] MOM's need-request data, almost entirely pre-Guidelines, and MOM's frictions reading (spoken, no number; mom_ps-03);

\note{[Short path] The Guidelines already set a process for requests. MOM's own survey finds that few who need an arrangement ask formally, a gap MOM attributes to frictions rather than employer resistance. % [P3]
What remains open is fit, in three parts.
First, high overall provision can hide which arrangements are on offer, and whether they suit the worker and the role.
Second, few studies measure together how workers value each arrangement and how employers weigh it in hiring; a Polish study is one. % [R16, L1]
Third, career worries, unclear terms and the effort of job redesign can block arrangements that would suit both sides; reasons for not asking are rarely measured.
For the partners, the question is which arrangements to make easier to try now, which to tailor by role, which to test before scaling, and what information is missing.
We use a simple map. [Full deck: first, where this sits in the research.]}

% Key findings (26 Oct 2026): a short preview of the results; the full summary stays on M-conclusion. Numbers: wtp_deck.csv main sample.
\begin{frame}[t,label=M-keyfindings]{Key findings}
  \FrameTop
  \begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
    \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{WFH}
      \BigStat{Navy}{12--37 points}{gap between what employers expect to cut pay by and what PMEs would give up, for 1--2 days, 3--4 days and fully remote WFH}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Common ground}
      \BigStat{Navy}{No gap}{for the compressed week: PMEs would give up about 7\% of pay, employers expect about 11\%; the difference is not significant}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Hurdles}
      \BigStat{Navy}{49\% vs 3\%}{employers' pay cut for 1--2 WFH days where most roles need on-site presence vs where few do; stated concerns do not reliably change it}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  \vspace{0.12cm}
  \Interp{Juniors have less access and know the Guidelines least; 45\% of PMEs fear a career penalty.}
  \SourceNote{Pay in \% of monthly pay, stated choices from unweighted online panels; preliminary.}
  \Backups{\BL{B-limits}{Limits} \BL{B-robust}{Robustness}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] A preview of the four results we cover. % [E1, E2, G1-G4]
For WFH, employers expect a pay cut 12 to 37 points larger than what PMEs would give up. % [G1-G3]
Only the compressed week shows no detectable gap: about 7 per cent for PMEs and about 11 for employers. % [Q5, M19]
Employers' concerns do not reliably change the pay cut, but on-site needs do: 49 per cent against 3 for one to two WFH days. % [M10, M12]
And juniors have less access and know the Guidelines least; 45 per cent of PMEs fear a career penalty. % [D6, M23]
}

\note{[Full deck only]
Flexible work is already common among the PMEs we surveyed: about seven in ten use at least one arrangement, and two in three use WFH. % [D1]
Staggered hours come next, at 27 per cent; the compressed week, job sharing and part-time are each used by only four to six per cent. % [D1]

Next, the choice task that lets us put a price on each arrangement.}

\note{[Short path]
Both sides chose from one FWA menu.
We surveyed 1,020 PMEs and 465 people involved in PME hiring or manpower decisions, from unweighted online panels; the firms lean large. % [S1, S2, S3, S4]
Each PME chose six times between two job offers; each employer, between two equally qualified candidates. % [S5]
These are the actual survey screens. The shaded rows are the attributes that differ between the two options; all other attributes are held at the respondent's own practice. In the PME example, offer A pays less and is staggered with one to two WFH days, while B pays more and is fully remote with fixed hours; the employer example offers a compressed four-day week, the same hours over four longer days, against fixed hours. % [S5, S6b, S7]
The pay differences between the options were limited by design, so rankings are firmer than prices. % [S6, EB s9]
For employers, this is a hiring choice, not a reply to a request. % [S5; EB s9]
Now the results, starting with PMEs. [Full deck: ``Next, how we turn these choices into values.'']}

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-employer-barriers]{Employers' biggest challenge: productivity, coordination, fairness}
  % F_fwa_challenge_m (scripts/fig_fwa_m.py): QID50 biggest challenge in offering FWAs, all 397 employers incl. Other
  \FrameTop
  \FigL{F_fwa_challenge_m}
  \Backups{\BL{B-org-view}{Employer view}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] Asked for the biggest challenge in offering flexible arrangements, employers name productivity and output quality (24 per cent), fairness across roles (23) and team coordination (23). Managerial resistance or lack of trust follows (14). Security and digital infrastructure are named by 6 and 5 per cent. % [B1, fwa_challenge]
The three leading items are statistically indistinguishable in this sample. The question asks for one challenge for FWAs in general, not for each arrangement, so it cannot say why a given arrangement, such as the compressed week, is offered by few firms. % [B1]
Next, do these concerns change the pay cut employers expect?}

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-concerns]{Employers' main concerns do not reliably change the pay cut}
  % F_org_concerns_m (scripts/fig_fwa_m.py; employer_splits.csv): difference in the pay cut required, firms that agree with the concern minus
  % firms that do not (points), all seven arrangements; filled = 95% interval excludes 0. Item-level p < .05 only for creativity (fully remote, staggered hours)
  % and productivity (staggered hours), not corrected for 28 items.
  \FrameTop
  \FigL{F_org_concerns_m}
  \SourceNote{Agree = 4--5 of 5; neutral or disagree = 1--3.}
  \Backups{\BL{B-org-concerns4}{Four concerns}\BL{B-org-view}{Employer view}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Full deck only] On the previous slide employers named productivity, coordination and fairness as their main challenges. Here we ask whether firms that share each concern expect a bigger pay cut. The answer is: not reliably. Group sizes, agree against neutral or disagree: productivity 244 and 221 firms, coordination 245 and 220, fairness 204 and 261, creativity 228 and 237. A fourth concern, creativity, shows the clearest signal and is in the backup (full figure). Across all four concerns, firms that share the concern ask for more in 24 of 28 comparisons, on average 15 points more for the creativity concern, 10 for productivity, 5 for coordination and 4 for fairness. For WFH both groups ask for large cuts; for the compressed week and staggered hours, firms without the concern ask for little (0 to 8 per cent) while concerned firms ask for 11 to 22. But only four of the 28 differences are significant at 5 per cent (three for creativity, one for productivity, all for staggered hours or remote work), and none after correcting for 28 tests. % [employer_splits]
Fairness is new here: it shows no difference at all. So concerns are a weak guide. Does where firms need people on site matter more?}

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-where]{On-site needs raise the WFH pay cut, not the others}
  % F_where_pres_m (scripts/fig_fwa_m.py from results_fwa/employer_splits.csv; scripts/fwa_employer_splits.py): pay cut employers would
  % require, all seven arrangements, by on-site presence need (137 firms: most PME roles need presence; 260: some or few). Fully interacted
  % conditional logit (group-specific pay slope); location p = .025, non-location (staggered, compressed, job sharing, part-time) p = .60.
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_where_pres_m}
  \Interp{Staggered hours, the compressed week, job sharing and part-time show no such difference. Early evidence only.}
  \Backups{\BL{B-org-splits}{All splits}\BL{B-org-other}{Other traits}\BL{B-org-view}{Employer view}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] We split employers by whether most PME roles need on-site presence: 164 firms say most roles do, 301 say some or few. Where they do, firms would require a much larger pay cut for any WFH: 49 against 3 per cent for one to two days, 60 against 30 for three to four days, 68 against 43 for fully remote. The WFH differences are large and the intervals are wide; this is a preliminary association from one survey. % [M10, wtp_deck, employer_splits]
For the other arrangements we detect no difference: the compressed week 6 against 11 per cent, job sharing 23 against 27, part-time 33 against 39; staggered hours are higher where presence is needed, 20 against 5, but not significantly. The intervals are wide, with 164 firms in one group, so we read this as no detectable difference, not as proof of none. % [employer_splits]
So on-site needs mostly rule out location flexibility, not necessarily schedule or load, and they are a more reliable guide than the concerns. Back to PMEs: do their values differ by job level? [Backup: all splits; concerns.]}

What PMEs give up for WFH does not differ clearly by level: for one to two days about 4 per cent for junior professionals, 9 for middle and 8 for senior management; for three to four days 9, 10 and 9; for fully remote work 14, 14 and 20. % [dce_emp_het, level]

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-why-pmes]{PMEs who fear a career penalty give up much less pay for WFH}
  % F_why_pmes, true size 13.0 x 5.0 cm: flexible job's % of choices at equal pay, 95% CIs, by career belief
  % (QID51_1 agree 4-5, n = 455, vs others, n = 565) [M4]; legend "No expected penalty / Expected penalty".
  % 1-2 WFH days 52 [47, 57] vs 64 [60, 69]; 3-4 WFH days 52 vs 69; remote vs a 15-45 min commute 55 vs 72;
  % location test p < .001 [M4]; compressed week 59 [54, 64] vs 58 [52, 63], p = .70 [M5]; 50% line (EB s3b)
  \FrameTop
  \FigL{F_why_pmes}
  % Note: F_why_pmes's former footnote. [M4] penalty = QID51_1 agree 4-5; "Associations" kept. Its second
  % [S1] 1,020 PMEs, 4-21 Aug 2026; [M4] fully interacted model, equal-pay shares, 95% CIs
  \SourceNote{Expect a penalty: agree (4--5 of 5) that flexible hours would hurt their career; neutral or disagree = 1--3.}

% note facts: [M4] 52 vs 64, 1% level; [M5] compressed week 59 vs 58, p = .70, no detectable difference;
\note{[Short path] Of the 1,020 surveyed PMEs, 455 (45 per cent) expect shorter or more flexible hours to hurt their career and 565 do not. Those who expect a penalty would give up about 2 per cent of pay for one to two WFH days, against 10 per cent for other PMEs; for three to four days, 2 against 14. The location difference is statistically significant (p = .002). For the compressed week we detect no difference (p = .15). % [M4, M5]
This is consistent with a visibility concern. We acknowledge that the career question was asked after the choices, and that part of the gap may be noisier answers. % [M6]
For firms and NTUC, appraisal by output could be part of any hybrid pilot.
So why do PMEs who want an arrangement not ask? The survey did not ask; we come back to that in the results summary.}

% ==========================================================================
% 19. DISCUSSION: A SYNTHESIS MAP BY ZONE   [full deck only]
% ==========================================================================
\begin{frame}[t,label=M-conclusion]{What we found}
  % Results summary (21 Oct 2026): four lines, one per block of results; no slide references here.
  \FrameTop
  {\FsBody\setlength{\tabcolsep}{6pt}\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
  \begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Values} & PMEs would give up \textbf{7--15\%} of pay for WFH, more with each extra day; employers expect \textbf{20--52\%} cuts, a gap of 12--37 points\\ \midrule
    \textbf{Common ground} & Only the \textbf{compressed week} shows no significant gap (about 7\% vs 11\%); 15\% of firms offer it\\ \midrule
    \textcolor{Employer}{\textbf{Employers}} & Name \textbf{productivity, coordination and fairness} as hurdles, but these do not reliably change the pay cut; \textbf{on-site needs} do (49\% vs 3\% for 1--2 days)\\ \midrule
    \textcolor{Employee}{\textbf{PMEs}} & Juniors have \textbf{less access} (80\% vs 94\%) and know the Guidelines least; 45\% fear a career penalty, and those who do give up much less pay for WFH\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabularx}\par}
  \Backups{\BL{B-limits}{Limits} \BL{B-robust}{Robustness}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] Four blocks of results. First, PMEs value remote work most, and more with each extra day: about 7 per cent of pay for one to two days, 10 for three to four, 15 for fully remote. Employers expect a bigger pay cut for the same arrangements; that is a hiring expectation, not a salary price. % [E1, E2, R10, S6]
Second, only the compressed week shows common ground: PMEs would give up about 7 per cent of pay for it and employers would require about 11, on the border of significance; the gap of about 3 points cannot be told from zero. The evidence is moderate and operating costs are unmeasured. For WFH the gap is 12 to 37 points. % [S7, Q5, M19, M20, G1-G4]
Third, employers name productivity, coordination and fairness as their main hurdles, but how much they worry about them does not reliably change the pay cut; where most roles need on-site presence, they expect a much larger WFH cut. % [slide 11, 12, 13]
Fourth, junior PMEs have less access and know the Guidelines least, and 45 per cent of PMEs expect flexible work to hurt their career. % [D6, M23, pme_level_access.csv]
We acknowledge that these are stated choices from unweighted online panels, and the employer splits remain preliminary. What do the results point to? % [S4, S5; EB s9 l.183]
}

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-discussion]{Policy directions}
  % Three directions (26 Oct 2026, PI request: fewer, specific, from our results). Letters link to B-optA..C. Old D (juniors) merged into C;
  % old E (measure what is missing) moved to the next steps (B-optE stays as a backup).
  % A: compressed week gap 3 n.s. (7.4 vs 10.6), offered by 15% of firms (71 of 465), written policy 17.8 vs 8.6, PME access 21%;
  % B: employer cut for 1-2 WFH days 48.9 (most roles need presence) vs 2.7; C: access 80/85/94, familiarity 29/52/77, career penalty 45%.
  \FrameTop
  {\FsBody\setlength{\tabcolsep}{5pt}\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.1}
  \begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.3cm}@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Direction} & \textbf{Based on} & \textbf{How to track}\\
    \midrule
    \hyperlink{B-optA}{\textbf{\textcolor{Navy}{A}}}\enspace \textbf{Pilot the compressed week} (same hours over four days) in volunteer firms, with a comparison group
      & No significant pay gap (about 7\% vs 11\%); 15\% of firms offer it, 21\% of PMEs have it & Take-up, quits, coverage\\ \midrule
    \hyperlink{B-optB}{\textbf{\textcolor{Navy}{B}}}\enspace \textbf{Add a role-by-role check of on-site need} to FWA guidance; start with 1--2 WFH days in roles that need none
      & Employers' pay cut for 1--2 days: 49\% where most roles need presence, 3\% where few do & Firms offering 1--2 days\\ \midrule
    \hyperlink{B-optC}{\textbf{\textcolor{Navy}{C}}}\enspace \textbf{Reach juniors and support HR}: put what is on offer and how use is appraised into company policy; brief managers on requests
      & Access 80\% (junior) vs 94\% (senior); know the Guidelines 29\% vs 77\%; 45\% fear a career penalty & Juniors' access, familiarity, career worry\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabularx}\par}
  \SourceNote{Stated choices from online panels; employer splits are preliminary.}
  \Backups{\BL{B-pilot}{Pilot checklist}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] Three directions the results point to; the middle column gives the finding each rests on, and the letters link to a back-up for each. None requires changing the Guidelines. % [S7]
A. Trial the compressed week. PMEs would give up about 7 per cent of pay for it and employers would require about 11, a gap we cannot tell from zero. 15 per cent of surveyed firms offer it, more often with a written policy, 18 against 9 per cent, and 21 per cent of PMEs have it. Operating costs are unmeasured, so it is a low-risk arrangement to test, not a proven one: SNEF could recruit volunteer firms to put it on the written menu, with independent evaluation of take-up, quits and coverage. % [E5, R5, G1, M16, M17]
B. Check roles for on-site need. Where most roles need on-site presence, employers expect a pay cut of about 49 per cent for one to two WFH days, against 3 where few do; PMEs would give up about 7. That compares one employer group with all PMEs, PMEs were not asked about presence, and the intervals are wide, so it is preliminary. FWA guidance could add a role-by-role presence check, and firms could start with one to two days where roles do not need presence. % [M10, Q10, M12]
C. Reach juniors and support HR. PMEs of all levels value WFH alike, but access and familiarity rise with seniority: 80 per cent of junior professionals have at least one arrangement against 94 in senior management, and 29 per cent know the Guidelines against 77; 45 per cent of PMEs expect flexible work to hurt their career. Employers' concerns do not reliably change the pay cut. Firms could tell juniors about the Guidelines through the usual channel, company policy, and train managers and HR on requests; whether this lowers career worry is untested. % [D6, M23, pme_level_access.csv]
B and C are exploratory: the presence result comes from the employer survey alone, and the career link is an association. For discussion: which of these could the partners take forward, and who could lead each? % [options evidence]
}

\note{[Short path] Three next steps for our research. % [options]
First, match firms and their staff: willing firms are linked to a few of their own staff, who consent directly to the research team. That lets us set what a firm offers and expects against what its own staff have and value, which the two separate surveys cannot show, and test the employer splits that remain preliminary. % [S4; EB s9 l.183]
Second, track over time: re-survey every six months and record hiring and departures, to see whether stated choices and offers predict take-up and quits, and whether values change. % [F1]
Third, test a manager guide on role-by-role on-site checks and on handling requests, given to a random half of firms first and the rest later, so that changes in offering and request handling can be compared fairly. % [Directions B, C]
}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-intl]{Evidence elsewhere: concerns and trials}
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9.5}{11.6}\selectfont}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.14cm}
    % [R16, L1] IZA DP 2023: 2.9% vs 21%, pooled; ILR Review 2026: 5.2% hybrid, 24.6% fully remote; Lead decision 4 (EB s14)
    \item \textbf{Poland, two-sided experiment:} workers give up 2.9\% of pay for remote work; employers expect a 21\% wage cut, mostly for lost productivity (Lewandowski et al., IZA DP 16041, 2023; hybrid and fully remote pooled). ILR Review (2026) version: gaps \ap 5\% (hybrid), 25\% (fully remote).
    % [P7, V6] six-month RCT, 1,612 graduates; quits down by a third; promotions n.s. over two years; managers -2.6% to +1.0%
    \item \textbf{Randomised hybrid trial} (two days a week; 1,612 graduates, one Chinese firm): quits fell by one-third over six months; over two years, reviews were unaffected and promotions showed no statistically significant difference; managers' productivity view: $-$2.6\% to +1.0\% (Bloom, Han \& Liang, Nature 2024; co-author J.\ Liang co-founded Trip.com).
    % [P4] employer-reported shares, mid-2024
    \item \textbf{Singapore firms offering scheduled FWAs:} 69.5\% report better engagement, 65.9\% retention, 59.9\% productivity (employer-reported, mid-2024; MRSD).
    % [L1] Barrero, Bloom & Davis 2023; Emanuel & Harrington 2024 (FACTCHECK F25)
    \item \textbf{Fully remote:} evidence is mixed and job-dependent; several studies find lower productivity, partly reflecting who selects into remote jobs (Barrero, Bloom \& Davis 2023; Emanuel \& Harrington 2024).
  \end{itemize}
  % [P7] co-author disclosure
  \BackToTwo{M-benchmark}{Literature}{M-discussion}{Directions}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-legal]{FWA request rules elsewhere}
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont}
  % Verified wording from FACTCHECK_REPORT F28 F31 F32 F33 (slide_patches.md s1); [P1, P17] Singapore; [P20] foreign law; [P18, P19] too blunt, acrimonious
  % Declutter: the full P17 wording (could include educational workshops) stays on B-guidelines.
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.10cm}
    \item \textbf{Singapore:} tripartite guidelines on the process, not the outcome; TAFEP takes an educational approach.
    % [P20] GB: Employment Rights Act 2025 changes due in 2027, not yet in force (DBT timeline, 25 Sep 2026)
    \item \textbf{Great Britain:} statutory right to request from day one (since Apr 2024); decision within 2 months; refusal only on eight listed business reasons; a tribunal if a request is not handled reasonably, not merely if refused. Employment Rights Act 2025 changes due in 2027.
    % [P20] Australia, Fair Work Act 2009 ss65-65C; New Zealand, Employment Relations Act 2000 Part 6AA; Workgroup s2.4.1
    \item \textbf{Australia:} eligible employees (e.g.\ parents, carers, 55+); written reply within 21 days; refusal only on reasonable business grounds; the Fair Work Commission can arbitrate and, as a last resort, order it granted. \textbf{New Zealand:} any employee; reply within 1 month; eight listed grounds; disputes cover process only. In both, most requests are informal.
    % [P19] acrimonious, Workgroup s3.2.2; [P18] COS 2026 too blunt, with its full object
    \item \textbf{Why guidelines here:} the Workgroup judged legislation risks an acrimonious workplace culture; at COS 2026, MOM called legislating the Guidelines, with a presumptive FWA right for parents of young children, too blunt.
  \end{itemize}
  % TODO(PI): re-check the UK DBT timeline (Employment Rights Act 2025) in Jan 2027 (EB P20, s14)
  % Check date: EB P20 sources GOV.UK updated 5 Oct 2026, DBT timeline 25 Sep 2026; EB s14 fact-check log, 6 Oct 2026
  \SourceNote{\textbf{Sources:} MOM COS 2026, FAQ; Workgroup report (2024); gov.uk/flexible-working; Fair Work Act 2009; Employment Relations Act 2000 (NZ).}
  \BackToTwo{M-discussion}{Directions}{M-question}{Question}
\end{frame}

  \FrameTop % first body token (centring; never a frame subtitle)
  {\centering

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-methods]{Equations and inference}
  % Simplified 2 Nov 2026: equation, the two definitions, two caveats. Checks are on the robustness backups; EB s3b conditional logit per side, SEs clustered by respondent.
  \FrameTop % first body token (centring; never a frame subtitle)
  {\centering\fontsize{10}{12}\selectfont $U_{ijt}=\beta_w\ln w_{ijt}+\sum_k\beta_k x_{kijt}+\varepsilon_{ijt}$\par}
  \vspace{0.04cm}
  {\centering\color{Muted}\fontsize{8.5}{10.2}\selectfont Conditional logit per side; SEs clustered by respondent.\par}
  \vspace{0.12cm}
  \begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
    \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Pay given up: $100\,[1-\exp(-\beta_k/\beta_w)]$}
      {\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont\RaggedRight PMEs ($\beta_w>0$): the pay they would give up for $k$. Employers ($\beta_w<0$): the pay cut they would require. Positive = a pay cut.\par}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Gap: employers' cut $-$ PMEs' give-up}
      {\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont\RaggedRight Positive = friction. The 95\% interval combines both sides' delta-method standard errors.\par}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  \vspace{0.12cm}
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.05cm}
    \item \textbf{Intervals:} 60 choice situations per side (10 versions $\times$ 6 tasks), so intervals may be too narrow.
    \item \textbf{Values:} employer cuts larger than the pay differences shown go beyond what respondents saw, so values are indicative.
  \end{itemize}
  \SourceNote{$i$ respondent, $j$ option, $t$ task; $w$ pay shown; $x_k$ arrangement level $k$. McFadden (1974).}
  \BackTo{B-estimation}{Estimation}
\end{frame}
% note facts: [S5] six choices, employer version with two candidates; EB s3b: equal-pay share needs no pay
% slope, 50% = no preference, read within each side; [S6] 17 to 33 per cent; EB s9: magnitudes model-based;
% [V1-V5] stated choices predict direction and ranking well, levels less well
% implication, spoken: partners can rely on rankings; per cent of pay is a rough size, never a pay cut
\note{[Full deck only]
This is what a PME saw; employers saw two candidates. % [S5]
A statistical model estimates how pay and each arrangement shift the six choices. % [S5]
We report one number for each arrangement: a per cent of pay, the pay gap that makes the two options equally attractive. For PMEs it is the pay they would give up; for employers, the pay cut they would require of a candidate who wants it. % [EB s3b]
We acknowledge that no pair had equal pay and the pay differences were limited, so per cent of pay extrapolates. % [S6, EB s9]
MOM, SNEF and NTUC can rely on the rankings; per cent of pay is a rough size, never a proposed pay cut. % [V1-V5]
Next, what PMEs and firms do today.}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-groups]{Women give up more for WFH; little else differs}
  % F_groups_m (fig_v2.py, 13.0 x 5.0 cm; compressed-week column removed, ROUND5_SPEC s4):
  % PME equal-pay shares with 95% CIs by gender, age (19-39 / 40+) and caregiving (none / any),
  % for 1-2 WFH days, 3-4 WFH days and fully remote (vs a long commute); 50% reference [s3b].
  %   [Q14b] every plotted group's CI lies above 50% for the three WFH levels (lowest bound: men, 1-2 days, 51.2)
  %   [Q14] women 63/67/73% vs men 56/56/63% (location p = .047, nominal only); age p = .30; caregiving p = .53
  %   [E18] 198 pairwise contrasts, minimum BH q = .70
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_groups_diff}
  % [E18, M7] null results are not equivalence (mandate: "Non-rejection is not equivalence")
  \Interp{Women give up more for WFH (clearly for 3--4 days); PMEs aged 40+ less for staggered hours.\\ Other differences are small or imprecise.}
  \SourceNote{}
  % Note (polish pass 7 Oct 2026): the 95% CI convention (formerly in the figure's axis caption and this
  % source line, [s3b]); "Fully remote: vs a >45 min commute", moved out of the figure's column title
  % ([E3] main model: fully remote vs onsite with a long commute; [S8] long = >45 min); and the figure's
  % former "* Nominal" footnote, verbatim ([Q14] the starred p = .047 is nominal; [E18] 198 contrasts, BH).
  % [S1] 1,020 PMEs; [E18] BH correction over 198 contrasts; [M7] 7 primary splits
\end{frame}
\note{[Full deck only] Each dot is the difference in the pay one group would give up and the other would give up, for the seven arrangements; filled dots have an interval that excludes zero. % [dce_emp_het.csv pairwise]
Women would give up 5, 8 and 8 points more of pay for one to two days, three to four days and fully remote; the three-to-four-day difference is clearly non-zero (p below .01), the other two are borderline (p = .08 and .06). PMEs aged 40 and over give up 7 points less for staggered hours (p = .02), and about 6 points less for the compressed week, which is borderline (p = .05). No caregiving difference is significant. % [diffs 5.0, 8.5, 7.6; 7.0, 6.1]
Two of 21 comparisons exclude zero, about what chance alone would give, so we read this as a suggestion that women value WFH more, not as settled. We acknowledge that no difference detected is not proof that groups are alike; mothers of young children are a small sample.
Only the career-concern split stands out, as we saw earlier. Why, then, is the compressed week rare? % transition to M-puzzle
}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-puzzle-main]{The compressed week: valued, rarely offered}
  % F_puzzle_r5 (fig_r5.py, 13.0 x 5.0 cm), simplified to the puzzle only:
  %   PMEs choose the compressed-week job 58% of the time at equal pay (55-62) [Q5]
  %   offered by 26.5% of firms with a written FWA policy vs 9.7% without (association) [M17]
  %   take-up where available: about 1 in 3 (65 of 210 = 31.0%) [M22]
  % "compressed week" = the same total hours over four longer days [S7]
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_puzzle_r5}
  % pilot framing: COMMENTS slide 16; mandate (voluntary, evaluated; not costless)
  \Interp{PMEs would give up about 7\% of pay for it, yet few firms offer it.\\ A voluntary, evaluated pilot is the next step.}
  % Note (polish pass 7 Oct 2026): the figure's former footnote ("+ All respondents / excluding one online
  % panel. Surveyed samples, unweighted.") with the deck's one dagger wording \DgShort [S1, S2];
  % [M20] cheaper option in 83.2% of PME pairs (1,502/1,805) and 90.8% of employer pairs (327/360)
  \Backups{\BL{B-puzzle}{Offering} \BL{B-pilot}{Pilot checklist}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] PMEs would give up about 7 per cent of pay for the compressed week and employers would require about 11 per cent with a wide interval and no detectable gap, yet only about 15 per cent of surveyed firms offer it. % [E5, R5, M16]
Firms with a written FWA policy offer it more often, 18 against 9 per cent, though a policy may follow offering rather than lead it. % [M17] association
Where it is available, about one surveyed PME in three takes it up. % [M22]
We acknowledge that the design usually made it the cheaper option, and a hiring experiment cannot measure rostering, fatigue or service coverage. % [M20]
So the case is for a voluntary, evaluated pilot, not a roll-out: SNEF could recruit volunteer firms to put it on their written menu, with NTUC co-designing safeguards. What happens when PMEs ask? % implication (who could act) and transition to M-barriers
}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-pilot]{A compressed-week pilot: checklist}
  % Fixer pass 7 Oct 2026, merging verified persona fixes: worker-02 (pay and leave unchanged; collective
  % agreements; voluntary for each employee, reversible without penalty; care hours; appraisal by output;
  % worker data only with consent; stop criteria agreed with the partners), employer-06 (for firms and staff;
  % fairness to staff who cannot take part; operating costs and coverage as outcomes), editor-06 (comparison
  % group), mom_ps-07 (bounds to agree), worker-07 (eligibility and fairness). Items at 9 pt and columns 0.34/0.24/0.39 (polish pass: 0.32/0.27/0.37):
  % at 10 pt (worker-02's fallback) the frame still overflowed by 1.28 cm in layout_sim; this is a backup frame.
  % [S7] compressed week = same total hours over fewer, longer days; never a shorter week
  % [B1] fairness to staff who cannot have FWAs: 23%, the top challenge at 200 or fewer staff (28%); [B2] 50% agree
  % it is unfair to offer FWAs to PMEs when frontline staff cannot have them (not printed)
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont}
  \begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
    \begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Design}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.04cm}
        \item Same hours, four longer days; pay and leave unchanged
        \item Legal, contract and collective-agreement review
        \item Voluntary for firms and staff; reversible without penalty
        \item Eligibility; fairness to staff who cannot join
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.27\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Safeguards}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.04cm}
        \item Service and coverage plan
        \item Fatigue, safety and care hours
        \item Workload spillovers
        \item Appraisal by output, not presence
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.37\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Evaluation}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.04cm}
        \item Outcomes: output, operating costs, coverage, retention, take-up, worker experience
        \item Stop and scale criteria agreed with the partners in advance
        \item Independent evaluation with a comparison group; worker data only with consent, never for appraisal
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  % polish pass (BKb): a hairline Rule sets the summary lines apart from the checklist; lines at the

\note{[Full deck only] Which results survive changes to the analysis? % [E15, RB2]
Dropping monthly salaries outside 2,000 to 50,000 dollars, the top and bottom 1 per cent of income or inattentive respondents, or adding a position term, moves PME values by about one point of pay and employer values by up to three; the rankings hold. % [E15, RB2, E11, R10]
But the pay differences shown were limited, so values in per cent of pay are model-based. % [S6, S6b]
We acknowledge two further limits: each side saw only 60 choice situations, so intervals are likely too narrow, and no cited study validates employer hiring choices like these. % [EB s9; V1-V5]
MOM, SNEF and NTUC can therefore act on rankings; prices need a wave with small pay gaps. What do the results point to? % implication (who could act) and transition to M-discussion
}
